endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Organizations should follow applicable human subjects research requirements, and best practices such as informed consent and subject compensation, when implementing feedback activities.

endorsements.title: The urgency of centering safety-net organizations in AI governance
endorsements.quote: Sustainably engaging SNOs and their patient communities’ could include compensating these individuals or their organizations for their involvement 45 , 46 .

endorsements.title: Commentary: Patient Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence; What have We Learned and How Should We Move Forward?
endorsements.quote: There are increasingly calls for these insights to be recognised and compensated, with the US National Institute of Health (NIH) National Health Council Fair Market Value calculator [ 15 ].

endorsements.title: Ethical Design of Data-Driven Decision Support Tools for Improving Cancer Care: Embedded Ethics Review of the 4D PICTURE Project
endorsements.quote: In the 4D PICTURE project, the ethicists and other researchers will work with the PPI boards on appropriate ways (eg, payment of the PPI boards) to alleviate the harmful effects of such structural concerns to help ensure that all voices are heard equally.

endorsements.title: Transformative potential of artificial intelligence in US CDC HIV interventions: balancing innovation with health privacy
endorsements.quote: Therefore, there is a strong call for community consultations, which should be fairly compensated, to create an inclusive approach to AI implementation in health.

endorsements.title: Perspective on patient and non-academic partner engagement for the responsible integration of large language models in health chatbots
endorsements.quote: When deemed appropriate, participant compensation must follow guidance from organizations with expertise in patient and public engagement [ 26 , 27 ].

endorsements.title: Real-World Data Needs Real-World Doctors: When Automation Advances Faster Than Clinical Workflow
endorsements.quote: To ensure AI implementation truly serves those it is meant to help, we recommend fully compensated [ 18 ] “patient” and “clinician-in-the-loop” team roles, with genuine voting power over co-created outcomes.

endorsements.title: Coproduction Without Youth? Closing the Participation Gap in Digital Mental Health Research
endorsements.quote: Many researchers in our YouthDMH Delphi poll (CA23153) identified a lack of clear guidance on reimbursing young people appropriately, generating anxiety about coercion and risk [ 45 ].

commentary.bottom_line: Seven sources, one federal framework and six commentaries, endorse paying participants in AI feedback and engagement work, but no supplied study tests whether compensation reduces exploitation or changes who takes part. The recommendation rests on ethical reasoning and research-ethics norms rather than on outcome data.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests compensation, and no study documents the hazard of exploitation in AI engagement activities. All seven endorsements are a framework or commentaries, which GRADE treats as expert opinion. Certainty that compensation achieves its intended effect therefore cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

NIST AI 600-1 frames compensation as part of following human subjects research requirements during feedback activities. This places the practice within existing research-ethics expectations rather than a new legal mandate. One commentary points to a fair market value calculator as a reference, and another reports that unclear reimbursement guidance for young people raised concerns about coercion.

One commentary on safety-net organizations suggests compensating patients or their organizations to sustain engagement, and another describes payment as a way to help ensure all voices are heard. These are arguments about who can afford to participate. No supplied data show whether payment changes participation by low-income, limited English proficiency, or younger groups.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare compensated and uncompensated AI engagement activities on who enrolls, who stays, perceived coercion, and whether participant input changes the deployed tool, along with work on setting payment levels for minors and for people receiving public benefits.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One endorsing commentary centers safety-net organizations and their patients, but the effect of compensation on participation from these groups remains untested.
